articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Chess is one sport where both the young and the old can excel

The World chess championship opened in Geneva with a game worthy of the occasion. Both the defending champion, D. Gukesh, and his challenger, Javokhir Sindarov, produced chess of top quality, and the draw was a just result . Given that the Indian was playing with black pieces and that he had gone into the match as the less favoured of the two, Gukesh could be a little happier with the game than his Uzbek rival. The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.

Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.summary: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up
articles.keyPoints:
• BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up
• Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.
• The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.title: Spinning wheels: on urban mobility in Karnataka
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Karnataka needs a coherent policy on urban mobility

While Karnataka has spent years disputing motorcycle owners’ right to carry paying passengers, Bengaluru — with the dubious distinction of having one of the world’s highest travel times per unit distance — struggles with inadequate public transport capacity and lacklustre intermediate options. The Supreme Court ruling on November 20 to dismiss Karnataka’s appeal was thus straightforward, allowing motorcycles to be registered as transport vehicles. The State has often called bike taxis unsafe, yet has not improved the prospects of safer options. Earlier this year, the Centre for Science and Environment estimated the number of buses in urban centres nationwide to be 70% short of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs benchmark and that 400 cities with populations between a lakh and 10 lakh altogether lacked organised bus services. In March, the BMTC reported a fleet of around 7,000 buses in Bengaluru, versus the 13,000 by 2025 envisaged by the Comprehensive Mobility Plan. Expanding the number of Metro stations also creates more demand for travel to and from stations, but the operating costs of the public transport corporation expected to serve that demand are not covered by the resulting increase in rail ridership.

Overall, Karnataka has struggled to set up a consistent transport policy. An expert committee recommended against bike taxis in Bengaluru for first- and last-mile connectivity and in favour of better walking infrastructure and bicycle rentals in 2019, only for the State to launch the electric bike-taxi scheme in 2021, then rescind it in 2024 over safety concerns and drivers’ disputes. The market for short booked journeys is also dysfunctional. But while allowing bike taxis could temper autorickshaw fares, the State must investigate drivers’ operating costs, the difference between the paid and the received amounts, and prevent large platforms from exploiting the market. Finally, while the Union Road Transport Ministry has reported that 46.2% of all road deaths involved two-wheeler users, two-wheelers’ safety relative to autorickshaws and cabs, by the number and distance of journeys, is unclear. The State should require aggregators to report injuries and fatalities and investigate the consequences of drivers’ earnings being linked to the number of trips undertaken. The Union government’s 2025 Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines already address passenger security, fares, and insurance while allowing States to authorise privately registered motorcycles through aggregators. Karnataka should exercise this additional power. A large national programme is required to address funding for public transport, which is necessary even when it is not immediately profitable.

articles.title: Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions

COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement , called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations ; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. articles.title: Just verdict: on Myanmar and the International Court of Justice
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Rohingya cannot return unless Myanmar turns democratic

On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy.

The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

articles.keyPoints:
• Rohingya cannot return unless Myanmar turns democratic
• On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy.
• The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

fullParagraphs: MEA spokesperson Randhir also addressed a report claiming China-sourced satellite data may have aided Pakistan in tracking Indian troop movements and monitoring installations during Operation Sindoor

The Indian and Chinese armies held high-level talks this month in the Arunachal Pradesh sector focusing on border management and addressing outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

articles.title: Beyond 26/11: Other major terror attacks in Mumbai over the years
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Here is a look at some of the other major terror attacks that have struck Mumbai city over the years, apart from the 26/11 attacks

On November 26, 2008, 10 Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorists from Pakistan arrived by sea and killed 166 people, including 18 security personnel, besides injuring more than 300 others during a 60-hour siege of Mumbai. The terrorists targeted several high-profile locations, including the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi Trident, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus and Nariman House.

But the city has been rattled by other attacks too, including the horrific 1993 Mumbai blasts. As Mumbai marks the anniversary of the 26/11 attacks, here is a look at some of the other major terror attacks that have struck the city over the years.

On March 12, 1993, 13 coordinated serial blasts ripped through Mumbai’s commercial and social hubs, killing 257 people and injuring more than 700. The city was still recovering from the communal riots of December 1992 and January 1993 that followed the demolition of the Babri Masjid on December 6, 1992, when the bombs exploded at regular intervals across Mumbai.
The attacks, the first of their kind in India, are believed to have been carried out in retaliation for the post-Babri Masjid demolition riots in Mumbai.

A month later, the Mumbai Police arrested Hindi film actor Sanjay Dutt for possessing an AK-56 rifle that was believed to be part of the arms consignment linked to the attacks. Although investigators could not establish his involvement in the conspiracy, his possession of the weapon and subsequent attempt to destroy it drew scrutiny. He was sentenced to six years in prison for illegally possessing automatic weapons linked to the consignment used in the attacks.
The alleged masterminds of the blasts, gangsters Tiger Memon and Dawood Ibrahim, remain absconding.
On March 13, 2003, a powerful explosion tore through the first-class compartment of a Karjat-bound fast local train at Mulund station, killing 11 people and injuring 82.

The attack was preceded by two other explosions. On December 6, 2002, a bomb blast at Mumbai Central railway station injured 27 people, while on January 27, 2003, a woman was killed in a blast at Vile Parle.

The first arrest was made by the Crime Branch in April 2003 when Saquib Nachan was taken into custody. Investigators later alleged that he and Lashkar-e-Taiba member Faisal Khan had masterminded the attack along with 23 others. Of the 25 accused, five, including Khan, later died.
Saquib Nachan, former general secretary of the banned Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI), and Muzammil Ansari, along with eight others, were convicted in the case.

articles.title: Maharashtra Cabinet approves free foodgrains for over 42 lakh farmers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Maharashtra Cabinet on Wednesday approved free foodgrains for over 42.30 lakh farmers not covered under Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), a ₹5,548-crore provision for the Narmada-Tapi diversion project in Nandurbar, confiscation of assets of firms involved in financial fraud, and a law to regulate private-aided schools, among 14 decisions.

At the meeting chaired by Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, the Cabinet decided to give free foodgrains to farmers who are not covered under the National Food Security Act in 33 drought-affected districts of the State. The beneficiaries belong to the Below Poverty Line (BPL) category.

“The farmers will receive five kg of foodgrains per person every month, free of cost, for the next three months. This will include three kg rice and two kg wheat,” stated a release issued from the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO).

With an aim to strengthen the irrigation system in Nandurbar district, the Cabinet gave nod to the Narmada-Tapi diversion project. This will include six diversions weirs that aim to benefit around 26,526 hectares with irrigation while generating 11.50 MW power, as per the Water Resources Department officials.

The Maharashtra government has also approved the plan to set up a separate MPID (Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors) tribunal with a time limit of 90 days for the disposal of cases. The Cabinet also decided to expedite the process of confiscating properties of institutions committing financial fraud and amend the MPID Act,” stated the CMO.

The State government has also decided to increase the hostel allowances for students from Economically Weaker Sections (EBC, SEBC and EWS) pursuing professional degree courses in health sciences under the Dr. Panjabrao Deshmukh Hostel Maintenance Allowance Scheme. It also approved the provision of financial facilities for teachers through RBI-registered institutions.

articles.title: India’s satellite supply chain ‘highly dependent on imports’, says space body
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: India’s space economy is currently valued at nearly $9 billion and is set to grow to $40-45 billion in less than a decade

India’s satellite supply chain is “highly dependent” on imports for critical components and the private sector’s contribution is limited to “structural assemblies” and “propulsion components” largely supplied by established public sector firms and vintage private firms, said a report by IN-SPACe, India’s regulatory-cum-promotional body for the private space sector.
While pointing out the potential of India’s private space companies, the autonomous body under the Department of Space underlined the challenges ahead.

Science Minister Jitendra Singh earlier this week said that India’s space economy is currently valued at nearly $9 billion and is set to increase to $40-45 billion in less than a decade, with the private sector set to grow from a a few startups “to nearly 400-500 companies in just a few years”.

The Supply Chain Landscape of Satellite Manufacturing in India report, which was made public on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), says that nearly 60% of satellite costs were attributed to electronic, electrical and electromechanical components, and specialised materials, many of which are imported.
India also has limited testing and certification facilities, which weakened prospects for acceptance in global markets.
Many companies largely operated on a “project-based manufacturing model”, which disincentivised long-term investment in automation and production capacity, the report noted.
Critical components often took a long time to procure – frequently 12-16 months – which led to project delays and hobbled responsiveness to market opportunities.

There was also a shortage of trained and skilled personnel in satellite systems engineering, quality assurance, testing and qualification, besides limited private-sector research and development and technology transfer.
The report was prepared by Brijesh Kumar Sol and Yudhishthir J. of IN-SPACe and “approved” by Pawan Goenka, IN-SPACe chairman.
The report isn’t a statistical survey, but paints a descriptive map of India’s satellite manufacturing supply chain.

articles.title: ECI directs states to correct erroneous entries in SIR rolls through Form 8 during ongoing Special Summary Revision
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The ECI move follows complaints of incorrect entries in several cases in the final published SIR lists

The Election Commission of India on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) directed that any incorrect or erroneous entries flagged in the electoral rolls during the ongoing Special Summary Revision (SSR) would be corrected using Form 8 after comparing the entries with the corresponding information collected during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
All the changes would be made after verification by the concerned officials and not through automated matching.
Form 8 is the ECI application for correction in voter details.
The ECI move follows complaints of incorrect entries in several cases in the final published SIR lists.
The directive was given to the Chief Electoral Officers of 25 states and UTs where the SIR has been completed and SSR is on.

The States and UTs are Andaman and Nicobar Island, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, Lakshadweep, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Puducherry, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, West Bengal, Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Mizoram, Odisha, Sikkim, Karnataka and Meghalaya.
The ECI had ordered the SSR of electoral rolls with reference to January 1, 2027, as the qualifying date in these States/UTs through letters on October 15, November 4 and November 11.

In its directive on Wednesday, the poll body said: “In order to identify and rectify any probable incorrect or erroneous entries in the particulars of electors (such as name, relation name or type, date of birth, mobile number, photograph, etc.) in the existing electoral rolls during the ongoing SSR, the existing electoral particulars of the concerned electors shall be compared with the corresponding information collected during the SIR.”
“Wherever any mismatch is noticed, the same shall be flagged for verification and for taking necessary corrective action,” it said.
In respect of such flagged entries, the BLOs shall visit the concerned electors during the ongoing SSR to verify their particulars and obtain a duly filled-in and signed Form 8, wherever is required.

📰 ECI directs states to correct erroneous entries in SIR rolls through Form 8 during ongoing Special Summary Revision

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

The ECI move follows complaints of incorrect entries in several cases in the final published SIR lists

The Election Commission of India on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) directed that any incorrect or erroneous entries flagged in the electoral rolls during the ongoing Special Summary Revision (SSR) would be corrected using Form 8 after comparing the entries with the corresponding information collected during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

All the changes would be made after verification by the concerned officials and not through automated matching.

Form 8 is the ECI application for correction in voter details.

The ECI move follows complaints of incorrect entries in several cases in the final published SIR lists.

The directive was given to the Chief Electoral Officers of 25 states and UTs where the SIR has been completed and SSR is on.

The States and UTs are Andaman and Nicobar Island, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, Lakshadweep, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Puducherry, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, West Bengal, Arunachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Mizoram, Odisha, Sikkim, Karnataka and Meghalaya.

The ECI had ordered the SSR of electoral rolls with reference to January 1, 2027, as the qualifying date in these States/UTs through letters on October 15, November 4 and November 11.

In its directive on Wednesday, the poll body said: “In order to identify and rectify any probable incorrect or erroneous entries in the particulars of electors (such as name, relation name or type, date of birth, mobile number, photograph, etc.) in the existing electoral rolls during the ongoing SSR, the existing electoral particulars of the concerned electors shall be compared with the corresponding information collected during the SIR.”

“Wherever any mismatch is noticed, the same shall be flagged for verification and for taking necessary corrective action,” it said.

In respect of such flagged entries, the BLOs shall visit the concerned electors during the ongoing SSR to verify their particulars and obtain a duly filled-in and signed Form 8, wherever is required.

articles.title: Karnataka High Court quashes postal ballot tampering case against former Chikkamagaluru DC, BJP leader Jeevaraj
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The High Court of Karnataka has quashed criminal case registered in 2026 against former Chikkamagaluru Deputy Commissioner K.N. Ramesh, Returning Officer Vedamurthy T.R. and BJP leader D.N. Jeevaraj over alleged tampering of postal ballots after counting of votes in 2023 in the elections held to Sringeri Assembly constituency

The High Court of Karnataka has quashed criminal case registered in 2026 against former Chikkamagaluru Deputy Commissioner K.N. Ramesh, Returning Officer Vedamurthy T.R. and BJP leader D.N. Jeevaraja over alleged tampering of postal ballots after counting of votes in 2023 in the elections held to Sringeri Assembly constituency.

Quashing the First Information Report registered in May 2026, Justice M. Nagaprasanna ruled that the inordinate and unexplained three-year delay in registering the complaint vitiated the criminal prosecution.

The court noted that ballot boxes were sealed and locked in strong rooms under strict police security since May 13, 2023, and were opened in May 2026 following the court’s April 2026 order on Mr. Jeevaraj’s election petition challenging the legality of election of Congress candidate T.D. Raje Gowda.

The court, while partly allowing election petition on April 6, 2026, had ordered re-verification of 279 postal ballots that were rejected during counting of votes in 2023 and recount of all postal ballots if any rejected postal ballots were found to be in order during re-verification. Mr. Jeevaraj was declared elected after completion of recounting of the postal ballots on May 3, 2026. However, operation of result of recounting was subsequently stayed by the Supreme Court.

Hours after declaration of result of recounting, one Sudhir Kumar Murolli, a counting booth agent for Mr. Raje Gowda, filed the complaint alleging that a crucial document, known as “ballot paper account” sheets, was tampered with back in 2023 itself after obtaining signature of agents of all the candidates.

“If there was doubt about the counting earlier in the year 2023, nothing stopped the complainant from registering the complaint immediately thereafter. With the declaration of the results after recounting in which the candidate loses and Mr. Jeevaraj is declared as a winning candidate, investigation by the jurisdictional police on a complaint cannot emerge. It is undoubtedly hit by delay. Due to delay, there has been lot of embellishments in the complaint,” the High Court said.

articles.title: Broad-based pressure on food prices continues: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: CPI inflation peaked to 6.1 % (y-o-y) in October 2026 from 5.5% in September 2026, slightly above the upper tolerance level of 6%–last observed in October 2024.
High-frequency data up to November 19 indicate continuing broad-based pressure on food prices, according to the November edition of the RBI Bulletin, released on Wednesday. .
Prices of all major cereals and pulses picked up. Edible oil prices recorded a broad-based increase, led by mustard oil, the RBI officials said in the State of the Economy article.

Vegetable prices presented a mixed picture, with onion prices rising moderately, tomato prices correcting sharply and potato prices picking up. The Indian basket of crude oil declined to $95 per barrel during November 1-18.
“The pressure on prices was primarily driven by ‘food and beverages’,” the officials pointed out.
Inflationary pressures were, however, not confined to food. Fuel and core inflation also firmed up, with 11 of the 12 CPI divisions registering sequential increases in October.

Within food and beverages, inflation rose across most sub-components, with notable spikes in vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats, reflecting positive month-on-month price momentum. Fuel inflation recorded a relatively moderate uptick.

Geographically, inflation increased in both rural and urban areas in October, with food and beverages inflation remaining above 6% in both segments. While most States and Union Territories recorded inflation in the 4-6% range, the number reporting rates above 6% increased.

On the external front, geopolitical instability in West Asia continued to weigh on the global economic outlook. Although crude oil prices retreated from their October peaks, the absence of a durable peace kept markets volatile. “Apart from extant geopolitical risks, the recent pullback in AI stocks lends uncertainty to the global financial outlook,” the officials said.

Despite the challenging global environment and hawkish monetary policy stances adopted by major central banks, the RBI maintained that India’s domestic growth drivers and macroeconomic fundamentals remained important buffers.
“The Indian economy continues to maintain the resilience in economic activities as evident from high-frequency indicators,” they said.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: “The Indian economy continues to maintain the resilience in economic activities as evident from high-frequency indicators,” they said.

articles.title: Net FDI fell to more than 5.5-year low in September 2026, as outflows jumped 40%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Despite September’s performance, net FDI in the first half of the financial year was more than 20% higher than in the same period last year

Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India in September 2026 fell to its lowest level in at least 5.5 years, with outflows exceeding inflows by nearly $5 billion, data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shows.

This was driven by a simultaneous slump in gross inflows and a jump in outflows. However, net FDI in the first half of the financial year (April-September 2026) was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
September’s net FDI figure of -$4.95 billion was the lowest since at least March 2021, the earliest month for which data is accessible.

Direct investment refers to the inflows that give the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production, as opposed to portfolio investments, which are typically more in the nature of speculative purchases of minor shareholding.
Gross inflows, or the total amount of direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September 2026, 46.6% lower than in August, and 17.6% lower than in September of last year.

According to the RBI, around two-thirds of the gross inflows were channelled into manufacturing, communication, and computer services sectors, with Singapore and the U.S. as the major source countries.

Total outflows climbed to $10.8 billion in September 2026, nearly 40% higher than in August, and 15% higher than in September last year. Within this, repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India grew to $6.4 billion, nearly 37% higher than in the same month last year, and the highest since at least March 2021.
Outward investments made by Indian companies grew to a five-month high of $4.4 billion in September 2026.

The RBI says that of the outward investments, manufacturing, and financial, insurance and business services sectors accounted for about four-fifths of the amount that flowed out of India, with The Netherlands, Singapore and the U.S. serving as the major destinations.

articles.title: Duty-free raw sugar imports up to 10 lakh tonnes allowed till March 2027
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The industry expects more imports in the coming days and this will ensure supply of adequate quantity of sugar in the domestic market throughout the sugar season.

Duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar will be permitted until the end of March 2027, according to a notification issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) on Wednesday.

A notification issued on August 20 had allowed duty-free imports of up to 10 lakh tonnes of sugar under the Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) scheme until December 31, 2026. Separately, the DGFT has allowed sugar mills time until September 30, 2027, to process the imported raw sugar and sell it in the domestic market.

The Indian Sugar and Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association Director General Deepak Ballani told The Hindu that price parity had prevailed over the past, making it viable for Indian importers to source raw sugar from international markets, primarily Brazil. Some imports have already begun.

The industry expects more imports in the coming days and this will ensure supply of adequate quantity of sugar in the domestic market throughout the sugar season. It will also keep the prices stable, he said.

articles.title: Air passenger services see 35% inflation in Q2; banking, securities transaction witness deflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The Commerce and Industry Ministry released the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27

Air passenger services recorded 35.52% inflation in the July-September quarter, recording the highest rate of price rise among the seven major services for which the inflation data was released on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Securities transaction services and banking services, however, recorded a deflation of 6.93% and 3.96% respectively, the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27 released by the Commerce and Industry Ministry showed.
The PPI has inflation data for seven major services — Banking, Securities Transaction, Insurance, Management of Pension Funds, Railways, Air (Passenger), and Telecom — with base year 2022-23.
Service PPI measures the change in the average prices received by producers on production of a service.
As per the data, inflation in Air (Passenger) Services rose 35.52% YoY in the second quarter, compared to 31.94% in the first quarter.
Annual inflation in the railway passenger service price index rose 2.17% during the September quarter, lower than 3.50% in the June quarter.
Inflation in 'Banking Service Contribution' was 3.86% in Q2 of FY27, higher than 2.62% in Q1. The 'Banking Service Price' witnessed 3.96% deflation in Q2, vis-a-vis 4.98% deflation in Q1.
Securities Transaction Service Prices saw a deflation of 6.93% in Q2, compared to 1.32% deflation in June quarter.

Pension fund management, insurance and telecom services recorded an inflation of 1.01%, 0.49% and 0.54%, respectively in September quarter, compared to 5.48%, 0.98% and 0.72%, respectively in the June quarter.
The government would eventually include more services in the Service PPI data.

The Commerce and Industry Ministry released the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27

Air passenger services recorded 35.52% inflation in the July-September quarter, recording the highest rate of price rise among the seven major services for which the inflation data was released on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

Securities transaction services and banking services, however, recorded a deflation of 6.93% and 3.96% respectively, the provisional Service Producer Price Indices (PPI) for the second quarter of 2026-27 released by the Commerce and Industry Ministry showed.

The PPI has inflation data for seven major services — Banking, Securities Transaction, Insurance, Management of Pension Funds, Railways, Air (Passenger), and Telecom — with base year 2022-23.

Service PPI measures the change in the average prices received by producers on production of a service.

As per the data, inflation in Air (Passenger) Services rose 35.52% YoY in the second quarter, compared to 31.94% in the first quarter.

Annual inflation in the railway passenger service price index rose 2.17% during the September quarter, lower than 3.50% in the June quarter.

Inflation in 'Banking Service Contribution' was 3.86% in Q2 of FY27, higher than 2.62% in Q1. The 'Banking Service Price' witnessed 3.96% deflation in Q2, vis-a-vis 4.98% deflation in Q1.

Securities Transaction Service Prices saw a deflation of 6.93% in Q2, compared to 1.32% deflation in June quarter.

Pension fund management, insurance and telecom services recorded an inflation of 1.01%, 0.49% and 0.54%, respectively in September quarter, compared to 5.48%, 0.98% and 0.72%, respectively in the June quarter.

The government would eventually include more services in the Service PPI data.

articles.title: Global climate talks must shut door on fossil fuel ‘clout’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The breakdown in the Antalya summit has deepened the crisis of confidence in climate diplomacy, making transparency and accountability in the negotiating process more urgent than ever.

The failure of the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, to agree on its central political statement, with countries unable to bridge their differences over fossil fuels and other key questions of climate action, has exposed the fragility of international climate cooperation. It should also sharpen scrutiny of who gets access to climate negotiations, whose interests they represent and what safeguards keep decisions accountable to the public.

The Türkiye summit ended without agreement on an overarching statement. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he shared the “deep disappointment” of many that the conference was unable to reach consensus on a statement that typically sends a policy signal to all nations. Some separate negotiating decisions were reached though. Nevertheless, the absence of a political consensus was a serious setback.

The breakdown does not show that fossil fuel lobbying caused the impasse. But it does make more urgent a separate question about the credibility of the process. A forum that asks governments to make decisions in the global public interest must be transparent about who is seeking to shape those decisions, what interests they represent and how conflicts are managed.

The international climate negotiations that take place every year still lack a comprehensive, enforceable system to identify and manage conflicts of interest involving powerful commercial interests, including fossil fuel companies and state-owned energy businesses. The Antalya conference has underlined why that gap matters.

The fossil fuel industry’s record of muddying the waters is well documented. A 2017 study by Geoffrey Supran and Naomi Oreskes compared 187 ExxonMobil communications between 1977 and 2014, including internal documents, scientific publications and paid newspaper advertorials. It found that as the company’s communications became more public, they increasingly expressed doubt about climate science. The researchers concluded that ExxonMobil had contributed to climate science while promoting doubt about it in its advertorials.

An industry team discussed a 1998 draft of the Global Climate Science Communications Plan at the American Petroleum Institute’s headquarters. The plan’s stated goal was to persuade a majority of the American public that significant uncertainties remained in climate science and to raise questions among policymakers.

This history matters because companies with large investments in oil, gas and coal have a financial stake in how quickly those fuels are phased down, which technologies receive support and how the costs of the transition are distributed. That does not mean every company representative at a climate summit is there to obstruct progress, or that attendance proves influence over a decision. It, however, does mean commercial interests need to be visible and the process needs rules to prevent undue influence.

The scale of corporate participation in Antalya brings the issue into sharper focus. An analysis by a coalition of non-profits identified 103 major polluter groups with delegations at the summit, including fossil fuel businesses, financiers and companies from other high-emitting sectors. It also identified 30 banks whose fossil fuel financing between 2021 and 2025 amounted to more than $2.2 trillion.

These are the coalition’s classifications, not official UN figures. They do not establish that the companies or banks influenced the negotiations. But they show the scale of commercial interests present at a conference whose purpose is to limit global warming.

Lien Vandamme of the Center for International Environmental Law says the problem goes beyond the number of corporate participants. Although the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) has introduced limited disclosure requirements, she argues that it still lacks a policy to curb corporate influence. “There is currently no policy to curb corporate influence within the UNFCCC process, and this is a fundamental problem,” she says. Once companies gain access, she argues, it becomes extremely difficult to monitor how they use it to influence negotiations.

articles.title: Wall Street roars back as Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Nvidia shares surged 32.2%, on track for their biggest one-day jump in more than two decades after an extraordinary reversal, which followed President Donald Trump’s call for Jensen Huang’s return

Wall Street’s main indexes rallied sharply on Monday (November 23, 2026), led by a ​nearly 7% jump in the tech-heavy Nasdaq, as investors rushed back into AI-linked stocks ⁠after Nvidia said it had reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive.
Nvidia shares surged 32.2%, on track for their biggest one-day jump in more than two decades after an extraordinary reversal, which followed President Donald Trump’s call for Mr. Huang’s return.
Mr. Huang resigned ‌as chief executive earlier this month over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
The chipmaker is widely regarded as a cornerstone of the AI trade, and ‌its sharp rebound helped lift sentiment across the sector after weeks of heavy selling.

“Huang’s return ‌marks ⁠one of the biggest reversals in the history of the stock market. Never has so ⁠much value rested on the shoulders of a single executive,” said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation.
“Wall Street envisioned a stock market without his leadership and didn’t like what it saw.”
The Nasdaq-100 was on track to add more than $2 trillion ​in market value on Monday (November 23).
The Nasdaq ‌Composite and the S&P 500 were on track for their biggest one-day gains since markets surged after Mr. Trump paused his “Liberation Day” tariff package in April 2025.
Chip stocks gained, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index up 13.4% and also on track for its best session since April 2025.
The rally was broad-based in ‌the tech sphere, with the so-called Magnificent Seven stocks Tesla, Amazon , Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet climbing ​between 5.8% and 12.4%.

Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran , whose huge pop hits include “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “The Reflex” and “Rio” and whose rise up the charts was inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.
Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.

articles.title: Fuel tanker crash ignites massive fire on highway surrounding Cairo, killing at least 30 people
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The blaze on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the Public Prosecutor’s office said in a statement
A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), killing at least 30 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the Public Prosecutor's office said in a statement.
The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the Health Ministry.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video shows firefighters working to put out the fire spreading amongst the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The Public Prosecutor's office said DNA investigations were underway to identify the victims.

Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene himself. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

Deadly traffic accidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.
In January, 21 people were killed and 16 injured in a massive multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

articles.title: Kremlin rejects ex-U.K. PM Johnson's call for a token Western force in Ukraine as unacceptable
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Russian officials have repeatedly warned that any Western troops ​deployed to Ukraine would be legitimate targets for Russian forces
The Kremlin on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) rejected former British ​Prime Minister Boris Johnson for a token Western force to ‌be deployed to Ukraine as unacceptable.

"What I'm talking about is a token as a symbol of our support," said Mr. Johnson. "The reason that matters ‌is that this whole war is basically about whether [Russian President] Putin can get Ukraine back into ‌the Russian sphere of influence, and what you ‌would ⁠be saying by having even a ⁠token Western presence of the Coalition of the Willing in Ukraine, backfilling, doing logistical stuff miles and miles from the frontline, would ​be, 'Look, Vladimir Putin it's ‌up to the Ukrainians to decide which countries they invite to send their troops to Ukraine.'
The Kremlin, which alleges Mr. Johnson sabotaged Ukraine peace talks in ‌2022 - something he denies - accused him of ​destructive behaviour.

"This is something that is absolutely unacceptable and intolerable to the Russian side – the ⁠deployment of any foreign contingents on Ukrainian territory. This has been stated repeatedly at various levels, including by ‌President Putin," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

"And we also know that, much to our regret, there have been repeated statements from European capitals and from Brussels regarding plans to deploy military contingents. I can repeat once again: this is something that is ‌absolutely unacceptable to Moscow."

Russian officials have repeatedly warned that any Western troops ​deployed to Ukraine would be legitimate targets for Russian forces. Dmitry Medvedev, a former ⁠president who is deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, on ⁠Wednesday (November 25, 2026) called Johnson a dangerous provocateur in a post on Telegram and said it was a ‌reasonable question to wonder whether a troop deployment of the kind he was suggesting would lead ​to a war between Russia and NATO.

articles.title: MEA separates Sheikh Hasina’s plans to return to Bangladesh from issue of extradition
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: ‘The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request,’ MEA’s official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said

The return of the deposed former Prime Minister of Bangladesh Sheikh Hasina, using a “travel document” to her country and the process of her extradition from India to Bangladesh were two separate issues, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026). Speaking at the bi-weekly press briefing, the MEA’s official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal made the distinction, while expressing concern over the prevailing law and order situation in Bangladesh.

Bangladesh’s request for Ms. Hasina’s extradition, made during the tenure of the interim government under Prof. Mohammed Yunus, is “being examined in line with our established processes”, Mr. Jaiswal said. Dhaka, in recent weeks, has talked about getting Ms. Hasina through an “acceptable prisoner exchange process”. Ms. Hasina had earlier this month requested the High Commission of Bangladesh, through a U.K.-based law firm, to issue her a fresh Bangladesh passport so that she could return home. Mr. Jaiswal said her plans to return to her country were separate from India extraditing her to Bangladesh.

“The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request,” Mr. Jaiswal said, adding that the issue of her return was a matter “between the former Prime Minister and the Bangladesh government”.

Ms. Hasina’s supporters from the Awami League have been agitating in her party’s strongholds in places, including Gopalganj and Narail, where the party’s workers have been targeted by law enforcement authorities. “We understandably are concerned at the incidents of violence against minorities in Bangladesh. We urge the government of Bangladesh to thoroughly investigate these incidents and bring the perpetrators to justice,” Mr. Jaiswal said.

articles.title: IAPEN summit adopts national declaration on muscle loss and sarcopenia
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Indian Association of Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (IAPEN), Chennai Chapter, adopted the Sarcopenia Declaration at Beyond Calories 2026, its national gastrointestinal nutrition summit organised in association with SIMS Hospitals in Chennai on November 25.

The declaration calls for early screening for sarcopenia, setting protein intake targets, regular strength exercise and early mobilisation and rehabilitation after illness, including post-intensive care follow-up.

It also emphasises professional education, India-specific research and the development of diagnostic cut-offs suited to Indian populations. It urges policymakers to include sarcopenia in national healthy-ageing and non-communicable disease programmes, particularly focusing on rural and low-income communities.

Sarcopenia is the progressive loss of muscle mass, strength and function. It can occur with ageing and is accelerated by inadequate nutrition, physical inactivity and chronic diseases. It increases the risk of falls, fractures, disability, delayed recovery from illness or surgery and loss of independence.

Doctors at the summit cited data showing that 43.6% of Indians aged 60 and above have sarcopenia, with 19.4% having its severe form. They noted that the condition also affects younger people, particularly those with chronic illnesses, poor nutrition and sedentary lifestyles.
The summit featured talks by specialists in surgical gastroenterology, critical care and nutrition.

articles.title: Air pollution accelerates dementia by reprogramming brain's immune cells: study
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The analysis found that people living in the most polluted third of areas are 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease or a related form of dementia than those in the least polluted third
Air pollution helps cause dementia by changing the genes that are switched on in microglia, the brain's immune cells, in ways that disrupt their normal functions, a new study has found.
The study, published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation , combined health records from nearly half a million people from the UK Biobank with experiments in mouse models.

"By recreating in mice what happens when people breath polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain's immune cells," senior author Sanjay Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at the Case Western Reserve University's school of medicine, said.

"These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world's population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it," Rajagopalan said.

Mice were exposed to outdoor Cleveland (US) air for five months. The fine particles in the air, known as particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), were concentrated to levels similar to those found in the world's most polluted cities.

Otherwise healthy mice developed memory problems, a leaky blood-brain barrier and brain inflammation. Their brains also showed a lower chemical balance reflecting its energy status and ability to withstand injury and disease.
The mice's brains also showed an increased death of newborn neurons in the hippocampus, the brain's centre for learning and memory.
The analysis found that people living in the most polluted third of areas are 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease or a related form of dementia than those in the least polluted third.
Further, in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer's, air pollution caused the same harm and also sped up amyloid plaque buildup -- a hallmark of the neurodegenerative disease.

The authors wrote: "These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice​ support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure."

articles.title: Meet the little stint: The tiny Siberian traveller visiting India’s wetlands
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Little Stint travels thousands of kilometres between its Arctic breeding grounds and Indian wetlands. But as shrinking mudflats and changing landscapes threaten its feeding and resting habitats, this tiny shorebird tells an important story about conserving wetlands

The little stint, a 25-gram shorebird, comes in lakhs from the Arctic to the shores of India, particularly to Point Calimere. “It’s an unforgettable sight,” says S Sivakumar, who has been involved in monitoring shorebirds in the Gulf of Mannar for over a decade. The birds remain through the winter months and depart between March and April, sometimes later in May. “In the 1980s, the little stint could be seen in several lakhs at any point of time. Even now, the numbers are still over a lakh as the Point Calimere Wetland Complex covers over 300 kilometres across coastal Tamil Nadu ,” says Sivakumar, assistant director at the Bombay Natural History Society’s Bird Migration Study Centre at Point Calimere, adding that such long-term observations help scientists understand how bird populations and their habitats are changing.
The birds remain through the winter months and depart between March and April, sometimes later in May | Photo Credit: S Sivakumar

The tiny bird’s annual migration journey, a feat of endurance, involves multiple stopovers across different landscapes, each of which must provide sufficient food and safe resting grounds. As shrinking mudflats and changing landscapes threaten its feeding and resting habitats, this tiny shorebird tells an important story about conserving wetlands.

Ashvin Viswanathan, scientist at Bird Count India , places the little stints as the most visible representatives of a special group of shorebirds that breed in the Arctic. “ This group is declining rapidly due to climate change and loss of habitat. Little stints too are declining in India according to SoIB,” he says, referring to the State of India’s Birds assessment. Their widespread presence, he adds, indicates the health of wetland ecosystems in India as well as conditions in the Arctic. fullParagraphs: The November full moon, known as the Beaver Moon, appears larger and brighter than usual due to its proximity to Earth

Skywatchers were treated to a dazzling view as the Beaver Supermoon lit up the night skies on Tuesday (November 24, 2026). The November full moon, known as the Beaver Moon, appears larger and brighter than usual due to its proximity to Earth. Here is more about the celestial display and when you can watch the next supermoon

The moon revolves around the Earth in an oval-shaped path (elliptical orbit). A supermoon occurs when the moon rises near perigee (the point in its orbit closest to earth), appearing larger and brighter than usual. This year’s full moon (November 24) is known as the Beaver Supermoon because this is when beavers prepare for the winter and also the time of year to set beaver traps before the swamps and rivers froze.

Supermoon appears 14 per cent bigger and 30 per cent brighter than a micromoon, which occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being near its apogee — the farthest point from Earth in its orbit.
The “Beaver moon” is a moniker for November’s full moon adopted by the Old Farmer’s Almanac , supposedly from Algonquian languages once spoken by Native Americans in the New England territory.

Though not a rare occurrence, supermoons only happen three to four times a year and always appear consecutively. Because the Moon is in its closest point to Earth, it can cause higher tides than usual, according to NASA.
Supermoon is visible to the naked eye wherever skies are clear and no special equipment is required.
The next supermoon will be on December 24, 2026. The last supermoon of the year, it will be the largest full moon.
The first supermoon of 2027 will be on January 22, also known as the Wolf Supermoon.

‘Wolf moon’ is a traditional name for the first full moon that happens in January. Many full moons have old seasonal names, often popularised in folklore, that helped people keep track of the time of the year before the advent of modern calendars.
Beaver Moon is seen rising in Chandigarh on November 24, 2026. | Photo Credit: SHASHI SHEKHAR KASHYAP

What if the plants choking the forests of the Nilgiris could be given a second life as works of art?An ongoing exhibition in Gudalur hopes to tell that story, bringing together conservation, craftsmanship and narratives of the intimate relationship between people and the natural world. “For all of us, sharing space with wildlife is part of everyday life,” says Rhea Antony, who takes care of storytelling and design at The Elephant People, a social enterprise based in Gudalur in the Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve that makes hand-carved wildlife sculptures, masks, and everyday objects from invasive plant species like Lantana camara and Senna spectabilis.
Handcrafted objects made using invasive species vegetation | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

The exhibition is an attempt to draw attention to the changing landscapes of the Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve, where the invasive species have spread across native habitats. These fast-growing plants suppress native vegetation, particularly grasses, affecting the food sources of wildlife and sometimes pushing animals towards human settlements.
ALSO WATCH Watch: How communities are rebuilding the Nilgiris ecosystem

The Elephant People collective works with Forest Departments of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka in clearing these invasive species. Instead of treating the recovered vegetation as waste, they transform the wood into handcrafted objects and sculptures inspired by the region’s wildlife, people, and landscapes.
The team includes over 50 makers across carving, painting, design, production, and operations | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

Titled Into the Forest, the first exhibition by The Elephant People features stories of wildlife, people, shared landscapes, and practices connected to the land. “These stories are brought to life through art and craft, with sculptures and installations created by a team of makers from the Nilgiris, for whom sharing space with wildlife is part of everyday life,” says Rhea. The exhibition features large-scale sculptures, smaller carved pieces, and interactive storytelling experiences. For children, there will be facilitated painting and story-building workshops, alongside interactive art installations that let them explore the forest through play. These installations offer opportunities to learn about different species, their habitats, and the sounds they make.

“Over the last three years, we’ve been exploring the stories of the Nilgiris and finding ways to bring them to life through art and craft. The region has been central to this journey. It’s wildlife, landscapes, people and the many relationships between them have shaped the stories we are drawn to and the work we create ,” says Rhea. While discovering stories of different species, they also learnt about encounters between people and wildlife, traditional practices, food cultures and ways of living that keep the forest at the centre. Some came from conversations with people, others from naturalists and researchers, and many from simply observing the fascinating relationships that exist within these landscapes.
ALSO WATCH Watch: A day at Baralikadu: Coracles, tribal food and community-led tourism
There are smaller objects like magnets and key-chains to large-scale sculptures and interactive installations | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

articles.title: All to play for: On the World chess championship in Geneva
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Chess is one sport where both the young and the old can excel

The World chess championship opened in Geneva with a game worthy of the occasion. Both the defending champion, D. Gukesh, and his challenger, Javokhir Sindarov, produced chess of top quality, and the draw was a just result . Given that the Indian was playing with black pieces and that he had gone into the match as the less favoured of the two, Gukesh could be a little happier with the game than his Uzbek rival. The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.

Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

articles.title: Beyond 26/11: Other major terror attacks in Mumbai over the years
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Here is a look at some of the other major terror attacks that have struck Mumbai city over the years, apart from the 26/11 attacks

On November 26, 2008, 10 Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorists from Pakistan arrived by sea and killed 166 people, including 18 security personnel, besides injuring more than 300 others during a 60-hour siege of Mumbai. The terrorists targeted several high-profile locations, including the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi Trident, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus and Nariman House.

But the city has been rattled by other attacks too, including the horrific 1993 Mumbai blasts. As Mumbai marks the anniversary of the 26/11 attacks, here is a look at some of the other major terror attacks that have struck the city over the years.

On March 12, 1993, 13 coordinated serial blasts ripped through Mumbai’s commercial and social hubs, killing 257 people and injuring more than 700. The city was still recovering from the communal riots of December 1992 and January 1993 that followed the demolition of the Babri Masjid on December 6, 1992, when the bombs exploded at regular intervals across Mumbai.
The attacks, the first of their kind in India, are believed to have been carried out in retaliation for the post-Babri Masjid demolition riots in Mumbai.

A month later, the Mumbai Police arrested Hindi film actor Sanjay Dutt for possessing an AK-56 rifle that was believed to be part of the arms consignment linked to the attacks. Although investigators could not establish his involvement in the conspiracy, his possession of the weapon and subsequent attempt to destroy it drew scrutiny. He was sentenced to six years in prison for illegally possessing automatic weapons linked to the consignment used in the attacks.
The alleged masterminds of the blasts, gangsters Tiger Memon and Dawood Ibrahim, remain absconding.
On March 13, 2003, a powerful explosion tore through the first-class compartment of a Karjat-bound fast local train at Mulund station, killing 11 people and injuring 82.

The attack was preceded by two other explosions. On December 6, 2002, a bomb blast at Mumbai Central railway station injured 27 people, while on January 27, 2003, a woman was killed in a blast at Vile Parle.

The first arrest was made by the Crime Branch in April 2003 when Saquib Nachan was taken into custody. Investigators later alleged that he and Lashkar-e-Taiba member Faisal Khan had masterminded the attack along with 23 others. Of the 25 accused, five, including Khan, later died.
Saquib Nachan, former general secretary of the banned Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI), and Muzammil Ansari, along with eight others, were convicted in the case.

articles.title: Maharashtra Cabinet approves free foodgrains for over 42 lakh farmers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Maharashtra Cabinet on Wednesday approved free foodgrains for over 42.30 lakh farmers not covered under Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), a ₹5,548-crore provision for the Narmada-Tapi diversion project in Nandurbar, confiscation of assets of firms involved in financial fraud, and a law to regulate private-aided schools, among 14 decisions.

At the meeting chaired by Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, the Cabinet decided to give free foodgrains to farmers who are not covered under the National Food Security Act in 33 drought-affected districts of the State. The beneficiaries belong to the Below Poverty Line (BPL) category.

“The farmers will receive five kg of foodgrains per person every month, free of cost, for the next three months. This will include three kg rice and two kg wheat,” stated a release issued from the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO).

With an aim to strengthen the irrigation system in Nandurbar district, the Cabinet gave nod to the Narmada-Tapi diversion project. This will include six diversions weirs that aim to benefit around 26,526 hectares with irrigation while generating 11.50 MW power, as per the Water Resources Department officials.

The Maharashtra government has also approved the plan to set up a separate MPID (Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors) tribunal with a time limit of 90 days for the disposal of cases. The Cabinet also decided to expedite the process of confiscating properties of institutions committing financial fraud and amend the MPID Act,” stated the CMO.

The State government has also decided to increase the hostel allowances for students from Economically Weaker Sections (EBC, SEBC and EWS) pursuing professional degree courses in health sciences under the Dr. Panjabrao Deshmukh Hostel Maintenance Allowance Scheme. It also approved the provision of financial facilities for teachers through RBI-registered institutions.

The Cabinet approved the draft Maharashtra Private-Aided Schools (Regulation) Bill, 2026, which will be tabled in the legislature. The move aims to provide a comprehensive law to be enacted for regulation of private-aided schools, the CMO statement added.

The Cabinet also cleared a draft bill to amend the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021, to exclude acupuncture as a system of treatment from its purview, the release said.

In another decision, librarians working in private-aided Ayurveda and Unani colleges will be granted revised pay scales in accordance with the recommendations of the Seventh Pay Commission, on a par with full-time librarians in government medical, dental and Ayurveda colleges.
